# Background & Motivation

\bluehead{1. Project background}

- During \textbf{COVID-19}, protective behaviours such as \textbf{mask wearing}, social distancing, hand hygiene, and self-isolation were important for reducing transmission.

\vspace{0.15cm}

- Compliance was shaped not only by policy rules, but also by risk perception, trust, demographic characteristics, wellbeing, and broader social context.

\vspace{0.15cm}

- These predictors may operate \textbf{differently across countries} because policy environments, institutions, culture, and public expectations vary.











# Background & Motivation

\bluehead{2. Research questions}


- Within each country, do the key predictors of compliance with COVID-19 protective behaviours change before and after mask mandates?

- Are these changes consistent across countries, or do they vary?

- Is there a set of common cross-national predictors, alongside country-specific predictors?

# Data Sources

\bluehead{1. Behaviour and policy datasets}

- \textbf{YouGov dataset:} This dataset contains information relating to individuals’ health protection behaviours, amongst other things

\vspace{0.15cm}

- \textbf{OxCGRT dataset:} This dataset contains the strictness with which the government has enforced its mask-wearing policy.

\vspace{0.15cm}

- Survey responses are linked to policy data by \textbf{country, region and date}.

# What Have I Done So Far?

\bluehead{1. Data pre-processing}

\vspace{0.25cm}

\begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
\begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}

\begin{itemize}
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35cm}
\item For the YouGov and OxCGRT files, various formatting issues have been resolved.
\item Mapped survey regions to policy regions.
\item Defined before/after mandate periods.
\item Defined two outcomes: Face-mask-wearing and Overall-protective-behaviour.
\item Cleaned the data:  Removing columns and samples with too many missing values, encoding the data, making column names more readable, and splits.
\end{itemize}

\end{column}

\begin{column}{0.38\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.68\textheight,keepaspectratio]{3.png}
\end{column}
\end{columns}






# What Have I Done So Far?

\bluehead{2. About Model}
\vspace{0.25cm}

\begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
\smallbluehead{(1) Random Forest}

\begin{itemize}
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.15cm}
\item An ensemble of many decision trees trained on bootstrapped samples.
\item Combines tree predictions to improve stability and reduce overfitting.
\end{itemize}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
\smallbluehead{(2) XGBoost}

\begin{itemize}
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.15cm}
\item A gradient-boosted tree model that builds trees sequentially.
\item Each new tree improves the errors left by previous trees.
\end{itemize}

\end{column}
\end{columns}

\vspace{0.25cm}

\bluehead{Why these two models?}

\begin{itemize}
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.18cm}
\item In Ryan's study, these two tree-based models were the strongest performers.
\item They capture nonlinear relationships and interactions among mixed survey predictors, while providing feature-importance outputs for cross-country comparison.

\end{itemize}

# Results

\bluehead{2. Train-test split}

The next step was to prepare data for modelling.

- I split the data separately for each country, policy period, and outcome.

- I used an 80/20 train-test split.

- Stratification was used where possible to preserve the class balance of the outcome.

\vspace{0.25cm}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Dimension & Values & Number \\
\midrule
Countries & AUS, BRA, CAN, GBR, IND, USA & 6 \\
Policy periods & Before mandate, after mandate & 2 \\
Outcomes & Face mask, overall protective behaviour & 2 \\
\midrule
Total modelling tasks & $6 \times 2 \times 2$ & 24 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
